#5635. Opendoor Says It ‘Rebuilt’ System With AI, Triples Home Purchases

After over a year of working as CEO, Opendoor’s Kaz Nejatian reported significant growth in revenue and market share during the iBuyer’s Q3 earnings call, and attributed the gains to a shift into AI infrastructure as the company says it has found ways to flip more homes without overpaying.

“This past quarter we rebuilt this entire system at Opendoor. We built an AI system that determines a specific repair plan for every single home before we buy it,” he stated. “Until August, our resale process was similar to literally everyone else in real estate. Pricing every home we owned basically lived in glorified spreadsheets with over 70 columns.”

As real estate incumbents have largely moved on from the iBuying craze that swept over the pandemic boom market, Opendoor has continued to push forward with a more nuanced approach to the model, offering a wider array of services to home sellers and partnerships with agents.

While acknowledging the company still has a long way to go, Nejatian is claiming the turnaround is working, even amid what he characterized as the worst years for housing “in a long time.”

“We’re winning the market without having to make riskier offers,” he said.

A lot of that comes from technology, along with a stronger focus on moving homes faster with less investment. Nejatian pointed out the differences between scaling with employees than with technology. He stated that increasing scale with the traditional method of buying homes involved hiring more employees, and a longer process.

“Rather than having people spending their days looking at pictures and doing mundane tasks, our people now each manage an army of agents,” he added. “In July, we had 5,400 homes. That’s 5,400 sellers sitting in a queue waiting for days for a human to confirm the price on their home. Two weeks ago, that queue was zero, and it will remain zero.”

He also homed in on the iBuyer’s new initiative—Buy with Opendoor—which launched in beta earlier this week. Although the Q3 earnings predates the program’s release, Opendoor CFO Christy Schwartz believes the initiative can open the company up to the broader market.

“Our emerging Buy with Opendoor offering can help buyers whether or not they’re buying a home from Opendoor,” she noted. “We see an opportunity to extend title and escrow to customers who aren’t buying or selling through Opendoor. Similar to listings, the offerings extend our reach beyond our home acquisition business and create opportunities to earn without taking ownership of a home.”

Previously, Nejatian came into the role with an aggressive turnaround mindset, touting an “Opendoor 2.0” initiative to bring the company back to significant profitability. The third quarter earnings may reflect the fruits of his labor, as homes purchased more than quadrupled.

“When a market slows down, companies are left with a cost structure and a system built for a different business. That’s the disease that Opendoor 2.0 is designed to cure,” he added. “That’s why I spend so much of my time on these calls talking about operator efficiency. When we say we’re investing in growth, we are building the capacity to handle the growth that will arrive.”

Overall, Opendoor’s third quarter saw a revenue of $1.02 billion, up 12% from last year’s revenue of $915 million and up 16% from the previous quarter of $883 million.

The number of homes purchased skyrocketed as well, increasing by 316% year-over-year from 1,169 in 2025 to 4,865 in 2026.

At the same time, though, Nejatian acknowledged the company is “behind schedule” on reaching profitability by the end of the year, blaming the slow market.

Opendoor’s stock fell sharply after the report, down about 17% at press time.

Again, Nejatian posited that the increases in efficiency with AI infrastructure have contributed to Q3’s results.

“Not that long ago, around 80% of the assessments we did on homes required an Opendoor employee, which could take many weeks. Today, that 80% is 2%,” he said. “In Q3, we purchased more than four times as many homes as a year ago, and our operation expense was basically the same.”

Operation expenses per acquired home fell to $4,000, down 36% from last year’s expenses of $6,300. The marketing expenses per acquired home dropped at a higher rate, down 57% to $2,800, compared to 2025’s $6,500.

Mortgage originations—or the process in which a borrower goes through to receive a home loan—increased over 400% from quarter-to-quarter, although the Q3 earnings may not reflect the full weight of the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in mid-September. While the latest data does show mortgage rates inching down slowly each week, it’s unclear as to when rates will go below 7%.

“Historically, most of our economics have come from buying and reselling homes complimented by title and escrow,” Schwartz described. “Our emerging mortgage offerings allow us to earn more from each relationship while meeting a critical customer need and making the transaction easier.”

Opendoor’s EBITDA loss also improved slightly on a yearly basis. Q3 2026 had an EBITDA loss of $31 million, while last year had an EBITDA of $33 million. The adjusted EBITDA margin also decreased, now at 3% compared to last year’s margin of 3.6%. While better than last year, Schwartz acknowledged that the latest data is still far off from last quarter’s EBITDA loss of $4 million.

“Most of the sequential decline came from the homes we bought in the spring selling into a much weaker market along with deeper price cuts as we chose to clear rather than hold,” she said.

Looking to the future, Schwartz expects margins to decline again in the fourth quarter, and states that they will continue to sell through the remaining spring acquisitions into Q1 2027.

She also expects revenue to grow by at least 40% on a yearly basis in the next quarter. Although revenue may increase, Schwartz noted that marketing does contain a seasonal aspect, and operating expenses will likely increase due to investments and growth.

“Comparing year-over-year, roughly a third of the increase in our expected loss is the additional marketing, and the remaining two-thirds is primarily higher holding costs as we’ve been rebuilding our inventory,” she concluded.

“Our goal is to be adjusted net income positive on a 12-month-forward basis at the end of this year,” Nejatian continued. “We’re a bit behind on this today, but we’re going to go through some walls and catch up.”

#5634. Kim Kardashian Snaps Up Palm Springs Estate During ‘Gummy’-Fueled Trip to Kris Jenner’s Home

During a recent visit to mom Kris Jenner’s home in Palm Springs, the star walked away with a new property.

It all went down during the Nov. 5 episode of “The Kardashians,” where Kim and Kris traveled with sister Khloé Kardashian and Kim’s costars from the upcoming comedy, “The Fifth Wheel”—Nikki Glaser, Brenda Song, and Fortune Feimster.

The group kicked off the getaway with some special "gummies” Kim had presented to the group during the private jet ride to the desert.

“I’m so excited because when Kris Jenner and gummies get involved, it is a recipe for success,” said Khloé.

When they touched down at Kris’ gorgeous La Quinta abode, the family members gave Glaser, Song, and Feimster a tour of the backyard, showcasing the hidden trails that connect the property to Kylie Jenner’s home right next door.

“We made these so we can all get to each other the back way instead of going the front way,” Kim told the group as they made their way through the hedges.

In an interview during the episode, Kim—who just so happens to also own a home in close proximity to her mom and half-sister—explained that the house between hers and Kylie’s was up for grabs.

She toyed with the idea of snapping up the estate so that the hidden pathways could be extended to a third property.

“Can you imagine?” she asked, noting that it “would be so much fun” to continue their “little backyard connections.”

After deciding she needed to find out if her home had a better setup, or if the listed house would be an upgrade, Kim went on to encourage the ladies to climb aboard her golf cart to “sneak in” to the yard of the available property.

The next year, Kim and then-husband Kanye West snapped up another undeveloped 2-acre plot in the neighborhood for $6.3 million—which would eventually become the home the Skims founder was looking to offload in the most recent episode of “The Kardashians.”

Aside from Kim’s exciting new real estate update, the family has another thing to celebrate—Kris’ 71st birthday.

The family showed her lots of love on Nov. 5, with Kim and Khloé sharing Instagram Stories showing the sweet moments before Kris blew out the candles on her birthday cake.

“I think one of the most beautiful parts of getting older is getting to know you in so many different ways,” Khloé wrote in another heartfelt post, which used footage from nostalgic family videos, showing Kris at home over the years.

“What I adore most about you is that no matter how much life you’ve lived, you still have this childlike excitement for what’s to come. You’re always dreaming, always evolving, always finding a reason to laugh, celebrate, or make an ordinary Tuesday feel like the most fabulous day of the year,” the doting daughter continued.

#5633. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5632. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5631. Massachusetts Plan for More Starter Homes Fails as ‘NIMBY’ Voters Insist on Local Zoning Control

Massachusetts voters rejected Question 7, a ballot initiative aimed at promoting starter homes by reducing the size of the lot required to build a home.

The initiative would have established a new minimum lot size of 5,000 square feet for single-family homes. The lot would need at least 50 feet of land bordering the street or public way, and it would also need access to public sewer and water, but otherwise, it would pave the way for smaller starter homes to be built across Massachusetts.

The measure failed by a slim margin of 50.6% to 49.4%.

"I think that, you know, there unfortunately is still a lot of NIMBYism throughout Massachusetts," says Mike Travaline, the government affairs chair of the Homebuilders and Remodelers Association of Massachusetts. The HBRA supported the measure, arguing that it would help address the state's 220,000-home shortage and allow builders to build more starter homes.

"There's a lot of resistance to any type of legislation or referendum that would take away local control from each individual municipality," he tells Realtor.com®. "Residents and town politicians really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Massachusetts has a serious lack of smaller, more affordable starter homes, which is preventing young residents from becoming homebuyers and keeping older residents locked into larger homes they can no longer afford to keep up.

The lack of starter homes in the state is part of an overall national trend away from smaller homes. The median home size in the 1960s was 1,500 square feet. By 2024, the median home size had grown to 2,205 square feet.

A Tufts University study found that approving Question 7 could create between 3,500 and 12,000 net new homes in its first decade and ultimately increase Massachusetts' housing supply by up to 320,000 units.

Andrew Mikula, the ballot initiative's organizer and chief housing economist at the Pioneer Institute, spearheaded the effort.

"We're grateful to have the support of more than 1.2 million voters who support bringing more starter homes to families across Massachusetts," he tells Realtor.com.

Currently, lot minimums are determined at the local level. A zoning report from the National Zoning Atlas found that over half the municipalities in the state require lots to be a minimum of 40,000 square feet—or about an acre—to build a home.

Those restrictive zoning laws are part of why Massachusetts received an "F" grade and was ranked almost dead last in the Realtor.com Affordability and Homebuilding Report Card two years in a row. The state was dinged for its complex zoning rules, along with its high prices, and high construction costs.

Massachusetts' median listing price is $699,990, around $250,000 more than the national median listing price of $415,000.

"From a developer perspective, we know that if we if we did build it, they will come," Travaline says.

"There's just gigantic pent up demand for that type of housing in Massachusetts because that housing really just does not exist in any sort of substantive quantity," he continues. "We don't have enough small homes that would appeal to first time homebuyers or young professionals, young families or empty nesters."

Travaline believes the bill was defeated because of pushback from local politicians who "really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Indeed, that was a major point of contention, according to Adam Chapdelaine of the Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposed the measure. Chapdelaine wrote in an op-ed that the proposed zoning law would "override local planning" and replace "thoughtful local planning with a one-size-fits-all mandate that ignores the individual needs of all 351 Massachusetts cities and towns."

Travaline says that many towns are concerned about how the passage of Question 7 might impact housing density.

But from his perspective, "it gives developers another alternative when they're buying a lot. Rather than maybe taking the risk that they have to build a really large single-family home on a lot in order to make their return that might have to sell for you know, $1.8 to $2.5 million, they could instead create two or three smaller homes on that lot and still make their return."

"Massachusetts residents, especially young people, are leaving the state to find a more affordable place to live, separating extended families and hurting our economy," Wesley Lima, of Legalize Starter Homes, wrote in an op-ed. "Requiring huge lot sizes to build a single family home makes houses expensive, reduces construction of new single-family housing, and encourages developers to build giant McMansions to recoup land costs. Anyone who needs a low-cost, single-family suburban home is all but locked out of the market."

Mikula says his next step is to "get into all the demographic data and kind of assess you know, where where we think, you know, policies like this can pass and then go from there."

#5630. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5628. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5627. California Passes Down Payment Assistance Plan, but Push To Cut Red Tape Remains in Limbo

California voters headed to the polls on Tuesday to decide three new housing-related ballot measures. While two of them handily passed, votes are still being counted on a plan to cut red tape and streamline environmental reviews for new homes.

Voters approved Proposition 1, which authorizes California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, permanent supportive housing, and affordable housing. The funding also backs both down payment assistance programs and mortgage programs for veterans.

Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed support for the measure, as did the Democratic Party of California. The ACLU, the California Apartment Association, and the California Housing Consortium also supported the measure, although there was some scattered opposition from Republican state legislators.

"This bond is about building communities, expanding access and affordability in California, where every family has a fair shot at a place to call home," Newsom said in a June statement.

Voters backed a similar measure in 2024 that earmarked $6.38 billion for homelessness and veterans housing programs.

"Higher mortgage rates have squeezed homebuyers and the for-sale market for four years, and they have hurt builders, too, especially in multifamily," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner says.

"Apartment projects depend on layers of financing, and assembling it has gotten much harder at today’s borrowing costs, particularly in a state as expensive and complicated to build in as California. When rates jumped in 2022 and 2023, a backlog of [COVID-19] pandemic-era projects that were already financed kept delivering homes. That backlog has been worked through, and the multifamily pipeline behind it is much thinner today," Berner adds.

Berner calls Prop 1 a "modest attempt to plug this gap" but only "one piece of the puzzle," noting that the infusion of cash won't do much to reduce approval times or land acquisition costs.

Californians also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income earners to purchase new homes. The state would issue bonds and use the proceeds to offer fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of newly constructed homes priced below $1.5 million

Borrowers must be California residents who pay at least 3% down and meet some income requirements. This, supporters say, would help lower the amount they'd need to save for a down payment on a new home. They expect the measure to spur the construction of new homes and be paid for when investors and home borrowers repay the loans.

The California Association of Realtors and the California Chamber of Commerce both supported the measure.

"Voters in California have seized the opportunity to help alleviate the burden of current mortgage rates on new-home buyers," says Berner of the initiative's passage. "With current mortgage rates holding above 7%, this presents the opportunity for buyers to save on interest payments for part of their home purchase, which could be a boon to the new-home segment of sales in the Golden State."

But, says Berner, housing is still above $1.5 million in many California metros, signaling that the measure's impact may be circumscribed.

"The median listing price for newly built single-family homes in the San Jose metro is over $2.1 million. In Los Angeles, it’s over $1.7 million. San Francisco has a median of about $1.5 million, and San Diego’s median is about $1.3 million. Among newly built single-family homes for sale in 2026 in the San Jose metro, just 41.7% were priced below $1.5 million. In Los Angeles, the share was 41.7% as well; 49.5% of newly built single-family homes in San Francisco were below the threshold; and in San Diego, 61.4% were. Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy."

Proposition 45 limits timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act. These new requirements would expedite environmental review and court challenges to projects.

Votes for the measure are still being counted. With 65% of the votes counted on Friday, 54.9% of Californians have voted against it while 45.1% voted in favor.

Affordable housing advocates—including the Associated General Contractors of California, the California Building Industry Association, the California Council for Affordable Housing, and the California Chamber of Commerce—expressed support for the measure.

Environmental groups and labor unions widely opposed it, arguing that it would reduce environmental oversight and community decision making around new development.

#5626. Smith Douglas Homes Grows Q3 Orders and Backlog as Margins Tighten

Smith Douglas Homes continued to grow orders and closings during the third quarter despite mounting affordability pressure. The challenging housing environment weighed heavily on the builder’s profitability.

The No. 33 builder closed 831 homes during the quarter, up 5% from 788 a year earlier. However, home closing revenue increased just 0.2% to $262.5 million as the average sales price of homes closed fell to approximately $316,000 from $333,000 in the prior-year period.

Net new home orders increased 13% to 777 from 690 a year earlier. The contract value of those orders rose to $246.1 million from $231.8 million, while the average sales price of orders declined to approximately $317,000 from $336,000. The quarterly cancellation rate was relatively stable at 11.3%, compared with 11.2% a year earlier.

Backlog increased 25% year over year to 947 homes at the end of September, with a contract value of $305.3 million.

“We continued to execute with discipline during the third quarter despite increasingly challenging housing market conditions,” said CEO and vice chairman Greg Bennett. “Higher mortgage rates and affordability pressures have weighed on buyer demand and profitability, but our teams remain focused on things we can control with respect to managing costs, building efficiently, and maintaining a steady absorption pace.”

While Smith Douglas Homes maintained its sales pace, profitability came under considerably more pressure. Home closing gross margin declined to 16.3% from 21% in the prior-year quarter. Pretax income fell to $3.3 million from $17.2 million, while diluted earnings per share declined to $0.07 from $0.24.

The builder’s lower average selling price highlights the affordability dynamic. The average price of homes closed decreased roughly 5% year over year to $316,000, while the average price of new orders declined about 6% to $317,000.

“While we expect market conditions to remain challenging in the near term, we remain confident in the long-term demand for affordable housing,” Bennett said. “Our priorities continue to be running an efficient home building operation and preserving our financial strength while remaining prepared to take advantage of opportunities as conditions improve.”

Smith Douglas Homes also continued expanding its community footprint during the quarter. The builder ended September with 113 active communities, up 15% from 98 a year earlier. Total controlled lots increased 2% to 24,724, including 22,693 optioned lots.

The company ended the quarter with 1,514 homes under construction, compared to 1,098 last year.

“Our disciplined approach to capital allocation and land investment remains particularly important in today’s operating environment,” said executive vice president and CFO Russ Devendorf. “Our land-light operating model, efficient construction cycle times, and conservative balance sheet provide us with the flexibility to manage through periods of weaker demand without compromising our long-term objectives.”

#5625. Fayetteville’s Growth Continues, but Affordability Is Testing the Market

The Fayetteville metro enters the final months of 2026 with several indicators pointing to continued economic growth. Total households are expected to increase 1.9% year over year to 236,740 in 2026, with annual growth of roughly 2% projected through 2028. Labor market conditions have also remained favorable, as total nonfarm employment grew 3.0% year over year to 311,300 in August and the unemployment rate fell to 3.1%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Several notable projects are moving forward across the region. Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is advancing a nearly $79 million terminal expansion after recording its highest monthly passenger volume on record in July 2026 and surpassing Little Rock in annual enplanements last year. In Bentonville, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine Whole Health Campus recently broke ground, an investment that could help meet rising health care needs as the metro’s 65 and older population continues to grow through 2028.

While demographic indicators and economic activity remain positive, housing market data tells a more mixed story.

Despite continued household and employment growth, home sales activity has slowed. As of July, annualized new home closings totaled 2,033, down 20.4% year over year, compared with an essentially flat decline for annualized existing home closings over the same period.

Pricing remains an important consideration. The median new home closing price reached nearly $380,000 in July, compared with $365,000 for existing homes. Despite that premium, new home demand remains concentrated at more attainable price points. In fact, the largest share of both detached and attached annualized new home closings occurred between $300,000 and $350,000 in July.

Meanwhile, single-family permitting is expected to decline 20.4% year over year in 2026 before decreasing another 15.1% in 2027. What was previously characterized as a housing shortage could become a more competitive environment as supply catches up with demand.

Fayetteville’s important storyline will be turning household and employment growth into qualified housing demand. The fundamentals remain compelling, but affordability and a shifting supply-demand balance are likely to separate the market’s strongest performers from the rest.

#5623. Columbia, South Carolina, Balances Growth and Affordability Challenges

Columbia remains a market defined by competing forces. Demand fundamentals continue to support housing activity, but elevated home prices, affordability pressures, and a cooler sales environment are creating some new challenges for builders operating in the region.

The market’s long-term outlook remains supported by solid demographic trends. Columbia’s population is approaching 890,000 residents, while household growth continues to outpace many mature markets. Household formation is expected to remain positive through 2028, providing a steady stream of potential buyers and renters. Meanwhile, median household income continues to rise, helping support housing demand even as affordability remains strained.

Adding to the area’s economic foundation is the presence of the University of South Carolina, which enrolled more than 40,000 students in 2025. According to a university study, the institution generates billions in annual economic activity across the region through payroll, purchases, and tax contributions.

While market conditions have cooled from the rapid growth period seen earlier in the decade, Columbia remains structurally undersupplied. Zonda’s analysis indicates the market is currently undersupplied by roughly 3.7%, suggesting that long-term housing demand still exceeds available inventory.

Builders have responded by expanding community offerings. Active projects increased year over year, with 109 communities currently operating across the market. At the same time, quick move-in inventory remains relatively manageable, signaling that builders have largely avoided excessive speculative inventory buildup.

Like most other markets across the country, affordability remains one of the market’s biggest hurdles. Columbia’s housing market is currently considered overvalued relative to local income levels, with home prices continuing to exceed income-supported pricing.

Still, the broader economic backdrop remains supportive. Employment levels continue to grow, unemployment remains relatively low, and household growth is forecast to continue over the next several years. Combined with the market’s ongoing housing deficit, those factors should help sustain demand even as affordability challenges limit the pace of future growth.

#5622. Bear Grylls Bought a ‘Derelict’ Island With ‘No Power’ and ‘Rats’ at 25 Instead of a London Apartment—Here’s How It Looks Decades Later

Bear Grylls made an unusual decision decades ago, when he acquired a marital starter home with his wife, Shara Grylls.

“At 25, just married, we bought a small, abandoned, off-grid island from an ad in the back of a magazine,” the British adventurer, 52, wrote in a Nov. 3 Instagram caption.

Grylls revealed that the purchase of St. Tudwal’s Island West cost them around $120,000.

“There were many who thought us crazy,” he continued. “The best adventures start with nay-sayers. Thank you Shara for being brave and saying yes!”

While the comment section had users divided over the relatability of purchasing an entire island—with one commenter wondering how “celebrities get so far out of touch from reality and regular people”—there were also a handful of people who stepped in to point out that even when adjusted for inflation, the island was less costly than the average U.S. home.

The “Running Wild With Bear Grylls” star explained the decision to the Sunday Times in 2021, noting that snapping up a Welsh island seemed like a more exciting use of the couple’s money.

“In 2001, we were going to buy a London flat for $288,000, but we bought a houseboat on the Thames [now sold] and the island together, and it cost less than the apartment. So we decided on the path less trodden and an amazing adventure,” he said.

Grylls shed some light on just how dilapidated the property was 25 years ago.

“The island had a 200-year-old lighthouse and two lightkeeper’s cottages, but [the houses] were derelict with no power, no water, no roof, and rats,” he said. “I remember my first bath sitting in 3 inches of water pumped from the old tanks we’d cleaned out. There was rubble everywhere and rain coming through, but it was a great moment.”

Considering Grylls has made a career out of his ability to survive in extremely harsh conditions, it’s not entirely surprising that he was able to get through a few rough years before the island would become a more suitable dwelling.

It took a decade to get permission to build a slipway, which Grylls said they finished just a few years ago.

“It has been life-changing for us,” he said of the addition. “Previously we had to keep a boat on a mooring, row ashore, and walk a mile up the beach with all the shopping.”

Eventually, the two lightkeeper’s cottages were combined into a single home with four bedrooms. But the island is still off-grid.

“It’s 20 acres and 5 miles offshore with no mains, electricity, or running water,” Grylls told Vanity Fair in 2012. “It has a little lighthouse beside our house and is surrounded by amazing sea cliffs, seals, and dolphins. It is my favorite place on the planet!”

To travel to the destination, Grylls and his family take a “30-foot, high-speed ex-lifeboat,” which he described as a “rigid inflatable boat with twin 300-horsepower engines behind it that can tackle any sea it needs to.”

He said the house is “as tough as you get.” Thanks to “2-foot-thick old limestone walls,” it retains heat in the winter and stays cool in the summer.

“But when those gales come in, you can still feel it almost shake,” Grylls admitted. “Sea spray reaches the windows despite the 150-foot elevation.”

While St. Tudwal’s may lack some of the modern amenities guests might typically expect, the Grylls family does “sometimes have friends” visit.

“They need to be up for an adventure and prepared to get stuck there if the weather turns,” he said.

Grylls has recently made headlines for his connection to disgraced former comic Russell Brand, who was recently found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Grylls helped baptize Brand in a ceremony in the River Thames in 2024, after the allegations against the actor had come to light. Prior to the baptism, Brand appeared in a 2023 episode of Grylls’ show, in which the pair traveled across the Hebrides Islands.

“Brand’s faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism,” Grylls wrote in a Nov. 6 X post. “I have attended a few now. Even visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes. It’s part of our calling as men and women of faith, to love and serve anyone. It is the sick that need healing.”

Noting that “judgment is for the courts and God,” Grylls added that “it is right that justice has now been served.

“I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day,” he said.

#5620. The chips are down: Qualcomm falls on revenue miss, weak guidance; Arm and GlobalFoundries do little better

Chipmakers Qualcomm Inc., Arm Holdings Ltd. and GlobalFoundries Ltd. struggled to move the needle today after reporting financial results that clearly left investors wanting more.

After an impressive earnings beat from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. just 24 hours earlier, investors may have had heightened expectations. But if they did, on a day when the market rocketed higher on the U.S. election results, they were clearly let down by the shaky performance of Qualcomm, which beat expectations on earnings but missed on revenue and offered weak guidance. The result was predictable, with its stock down more than 6% after-hours.

Both Arm and GlobalFoundries did better, but it wasn’t enough to satisfy investors who are becoming increasingly concerned about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence industry that has driven significant growth for all three chipmakers over the last couple of years.

The biggest disappointment was Qualcomm, which reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.17 per share on revenue of $10.44 billion, up just 8% from a year earlier. The results were mixed, with Wall Street looking for earnings of $2.16 per share on sales of $10.48 billion. For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it’s looking for earnings of around $2.25 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range on sales of $10.48 billion, falling short of the Street’s target of $2.27 per share in earnings and $10.48 billion in revenue.

Qualcomm’s troubles stem from the fact that it has less exposure to the AI industry’s rampant growth than many other chipmakers. The bulk of its sales comes from system-on-chips and modems for smartphones. But the market is currently reeling due to the rising cost of components such as memory, which have forced handset makers to bump up their prices, reducing demand. Qualcomm has tried to weather the storm by raising the prices of its own chips recently, but its smartphone chip sales fell 26% in the quarter to just $5.14 billion, well behind the Street’s target of $5.21 billion.

Under Chief Executive Cristiano Amon (pictured), Qualcomm has tried to pivot and grow its position in alternative chip markets, particularly the AI data center industry. Revenue from that segment rose to $650 million during the quarter, but it’s still dwarfed by the smartphone business.

Nonetheless, Amon insisted that the company will grow its data center business to more than $5 billion in revenue by the end of fiscal 2027. He said the company recently struck a deal with an unnamed global hyperscaler for optical connectivity chips. “We don’t have a demand issue; it’s a supply issue,” he told analysts on a conference call. “If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better.”

Qualcomm’s automotive business was a bright spot, with sales there rising 89% to $1.99 billion in the quarter, above the Street’s consensus estimate of $1.66 billion. Internet of Things revenue came to $1.88 billion, up 4% from a year ago and just ahead of the Street’s estimate.

Finally, there’s Qualcomm’s QTL business, which generates revenue from licensing intellectual property for modems, 5G connectivity and other technologies. That segment added $1.3 billion in revenue, down 7%, despite signing renewed licensing agreements with Apple Inc., Transsion Inc. and Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd.

Chip design company Arm delivered much more palatable results, but it was somewhat cautious with its guidance for the current quarter, and its stock was down 2% in late trading today. The company reported adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, just beating the Street’s target of 48 cents, while revenue rose 27% from a year earlier, to $1.44 billion, ahead of the $1.38 billion analyst estimate.

Unlike Qualcomm, Arm doesn’t manufacture complete chips for its customers, but instead designs and licenses processor blueprints for customers such as Apple Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Qualcomm to build their own custom chips. Where Arm is more similar to Qualcomm is in its strategy, where it too is also pivoting to focus on data center chip designs, trying to tap into the demand for AI compute. Arm said its data center business was the main growth driver this year, with royalties there doubling year-over-year.

However, Arm’s guidance did little to excite investors. The company said it’s looking for earnings of 56 cents per share, plus or minus four cents, compared with Wall Street’s forecast of 55 cents per share. For revenue, it’s targeting $1.54 billion, plus or minus $50 million, which is just ahead of the Street’s $1.52 billion target.

GlobalFoundries did a little better than its peers today, posting results and guidance for the current that squeaked past expectations. However, its stock remained flat after-hours.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on sales of $1.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, with growth driven by strong demand from AI and data center customers, it said. The results were better than expected, with analysts targeting earnings of 51 cents on revenue of $1.89 billion.

GlobalFoundries’ also differs from Qualcomm, in that it’s a pure-play contract manufacturer that builds the processors designed by semiconductors firms, rather than designing chips itself or selling them under its own brand. Qualcomm is actually one of its biggest customers, alongside Broadcom Inc., NXP Semiconductors N.V. and Infineon Technologies Inc. As such, its fortunes are very much aligned with those of the chip designers it caters too.

For the current quarter, GlobalFoundries said it’s looking for earnings of 59 cents per share, plus or minus five cents, on revenue of about $2 billion. Wall Street is looking for earnings of 57 cents per share and has the same revenue target.

#5619. Johnson Development’s Jubilee Earns the First WELL Residence Certifications in Texas

The International Well Building Institute (IWBI) has recently awarded 185 homes in Jubilee a WELL Residence certification. The 1,622-acre community by Johnson Development is the first in Texas to have homes receive the certification.

Signifying they have met a global standard for healthier, more resilient homes, the 185 residences represent 478,493 square feet of development and is the second group of Jubilee homes to receive WELL certification, with 125 homes earning the designation last year.

“We’re always excited about these certifications because they provide third-party recognition that we are actually building a community that truly prioritizes wellness and isn’t simply a marketing pitch,” said Nick Deacon, Jubilee Development manager. “Having the respected independent IWBI validate our efforts makes the achievement that much more meaningful.”

Up from the minimum 40 criteria used to certify homes last year, the homes met 45 criteria to earn their certifications. Categories considered span from air and water quality to light, sound, and thermal comfort.

Deacon added, “It’s encouraging to see us continuing to build on what we learned from our first submission.” Another 215 homes have been submitted for certification with the goal to have all homes in Jubilee earn the WELL Residence seal.

Jubilee was the first Texas community to become an early adopter of IWBI’s WELL for residential program in 2023. Today, 4,470 units around the world representing 6,820,597 square feet have received a WELL Residence certification, according to IBWI. Johnson Development was one of 25 early adopters across 10 countries.

Every home in Jubilee is built with a variety of wellness features, including a reverse-osmosis filtration system at the kitchen sink; a fresh-air intake and a MERV 13 media filter; circadian rhythm lighting for the family room, kitchen, and primary bedroom; and a central automation system.

“Your home—your community—should be your sanctuary,” Deacon said. “Jubilee is designed to be just that, a place where you can rejuvenate, relax, and take comfort.”

Builders include Beazer Homes, Chesmar, Coventry Homes, David Weekley Homes, Highland Homes, J. Patrick Homes, Newmark Homes, Perry Homes, Tri Pointe Homes, and Westin Homes.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5618. The 2027 Paint Colors of the Year Take an Emotional Turn

In the past, one hue typically dominated paint colors of the year, with different brands interpreting the color. For 2027, while there are a few blues and greens on offer, there is a much wider variety. Themes are less color-specific and more about emotional intent.

“Color has always been tied to emotion. We instinctively use it to create spaces that make us feel a certain way, and the colors we choose often reflect what we’re looking for in our lives,” says Lisbeth Parada, color marketing manager for Dutch Boy and Minwax brands.

​In 2027, that’s digital detox, permission to be authentic, and the opportunity for stillness and reflection.

​“We’re living in a world increasingly shaped by technology, algorithms, and an almost constant stream of information telling us what to think, what to buy, and how to live. We sense a growing desire to reconnect with our own instincts and the tangible experiences that make us feel human,” says Phillipa Radon, interior designer and C2 paint color specialist.

This year’s color trends tell us it’s not enough to treat home as a retreat anymore; recharging is necessary too, to manage the fast pace of the world around us. The variety of colors suggests multiple ways to gather that energy, with consumers choosing what resonates with them.

In new-construction homes, color choice is even more important, with paint offering homeowners a powerful way to personalize a brand-new space and forge that emotional connection to restoration.

​Here are the paint colors of the year for 2027.

​Sometimes paint color names are intentionally vague as part of their marketing micro-story. Not BEHR’s Grounded, with a name and a mossy green color that instantly frame the experience.

Its name has a double meaning too, as an invitation to breathe and get back to basics, amid digital overwhelm.

“What makes Grounded so relevant as BEHR’s 2027 Color of the Year is the way it balances two things people increasingly want from their homes: calm, and a feeling of life,” says Kayla Kratz, head of color at BEHR.

She notes that for many years, that meant paring down to a minimalist aesthetic, but today’s homeowners want more warmth and personality.

“Grounded answers that shift. The moss and olive tones bring a natural vitality, while warm brown undertones add depth and steadiness. The result is restorative without being static.”

Kratz says that the color replicates the dynamic greens of a forest, evolving throughout the day and changing light conditions.

​Deep Rooted, a nature-inspired warm orange, is energetic but steady and reassuring.

​“There’s an optimistic quality to the color. It has enough richness and energy to support bold contrasts and individual expression. The name brings those ideas together: feeling rooted while remaining open to possibility, and Deep Rooted captures that balance,” says Parada.

​It’s a perfect example of how paint color names are shaping the experience this year, with this color meant to encourage strength by standing still, not always easily done in today’s fast pace of living.

“​The paint color name captures both the color’s connection to nature and the sense of grounding many people want their homes to provide. At home, that translates into spaces that feel personal, welcoming, and comfortably lived in,” says Parada.

​Artifact is a smoky, atmospheric blue intended to create space to pause, recalibrate, and think more clearly after you’ve had a chance to catch your breath. These moments in time are both treasured and rare, which is reflected in the paint color name.

Artifact also embraces the idea of authorship, and how major change doesn’t necessarily require a makeover.

​“As consumers move away from creating homes that look like everyone else’s, they’re focusing on spaces that reflect who they are, where they’ve been, and what matters most to them, “ says Ashley McCollum, color marketing manager at Glidden.

​“People don’t necessarily want to reinvent themselves or start from scratch but rather make thoughtful adjustments that help their life feel more balanced and manageable,” says McCollum.

​“Artifact is not a reinvention, but a readjustment. It brings a sense of ease and relaxation after a busy day, helping you to unwind and feel more grounded. As a mid-tone, smoky blue, it leans warmer and has depth that strikes a balance between focus and comfort.”

This calming blue is nuanced and versatile, the kind of color that’s felt before it is seen, making it a good choice for homeowners who are choosing colors for an emotional impact.

Celery is a light green with yellow undertones that feels more herbal than botanical. It’s fresh and lively, marking a transition for Sherwin-Williams’ color trends.

Their paint color of the year last year was Universal Khaki, inspired by nostalgia and the comfort found in familiarity. Celery takes that feel-good energy into the future on a positive note. The color emerges alongside consumers’ appetite for expressive colors and a continued focus on wellness design.

A few paint colors of the year for 2027 are green, a carryover from last year’s color trends, but Celery offers a different perspective.

“While deeper, earthier greens have helped create grounded, restorative spaces, we’re beginning to see that nature-inspired palette evolve in a more expressive and optimistic direction,” says Ashley Banbury, color market manager at Sherwin-Williams.

“Celery reflects this shift, bringing a lighter, more playful energy to a color family that homeowners already know and love. It shows that green can be both calming and invigorating, offering a fresh perspective on nature-inspired design while encouraging homeowners to embrace color in more personal and unexpected ways,” says Banbury.

C2’s Pueblo is one of the more dynamic colors this year, with its identity shaped by an intentional refusal to commit to a single hue.

“What makes Pueblo so fascinating is that it resists a single definition. At its heart, it’s a warm, muted rose that bridges the space between deep floral tones and earthy neutrals. Its nuanced undertones interact with the changing temperature and intensity of natural light, revealing different aspects of the color throughout the day,” says Radon.

​“That complexity brings an unusual sense of dimension to an interior. Rather than creating a static backdrop, Pueblo becomes part of the experience of living in a space.”

​In the context of this year’s color themes, Pueblo taps into the idea that creativity and movement create energy to digitally detox.

​“There’s a certain confidence in choosing a color like that. It suggests we’re ready to move beyond simply creating a sanctuary and begin using our homes as places for creativity, individuality, and renewed engagement with life,” Radon says.

​Benjamin Moore has gone all-in on timeless over trends this year with their choice of Webster Green, a classic forest green that the paint brand is betting has staying power, given how prevalent various shades of green have been in color trends over the last few years.

​Green is adaptable and inherently energizing, which makes this shade a relevant tool for homeowners who want something sturdy but stylish too. Timeless design and decor choices are becoming more important to homeowners, for the sake of affordability and sustainability too.

​“Webster Green reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy. Its composed nature feels both rooted and forward-looking, while enhancing spaces that feel distinctive, collected, and continually new,” says Andrea Magno, vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing, at Benjamin Moore.​

​A sultry brown with plum undertones, French Press Coffee is all about striking the right mood and elevating daily rituals, another approach to gathering energy ahead of the daily grind. It’s the color equivalent to providing time and space to savor a hot, highly flavorful cup of coffee.

​It’s a little more nuanced than some of the other moody hues released in years prior, thanks to multidimensional color that adds visual weight and interest, while broadening potential applications.

​”French Press Coffee is the kind of color that reveals itself gradually,” said Lauren Hoferkamp, color marketing manager at Dunn-Edwards. “As light shifts throughout the day, its subtle plum undertone emerges, adding complexity you don’t always see in a neutral. It’s grounding and restrained yet full of character.”

Blues dominated 2023’s colors of the year for their spa-inspired calm, and Valspar is rekindling those vibes. Chosen for being familiar but fresh, Cottage Door is a mid-toned blue with warm undertones.

Sue Kim, director of color marketing at Valspar, says that the color, “is reflective and warm, with timeless appeal that feels personal and grounding. Cottage Door captures blue’s natural sense of security and trust while serving as a colorful new neutral that layers effortlessly into the home. It creates spaces that feel balanced, comforting, and inviting.”

The color taps into consumers’ increasingly pragmatic view on home design, and the company touts it as “designed for real life.” Homeowners would rather choose a color that endures than redecorate tomorrow.

#5617. Kourtney Kardashian Slams ‘Fabricated’ Rumors That She Doesn’t Live With Travis Barker and Shares ‘Really Vulnerable’ Renovation of Calabasas Home

Kourtney Kardashian is setting the record straight on her living arrangements with her husband, Travis Barker.

On the Nov. 5 episode of "The Kardashians," the Poosh founder is seen driving around town with her close friend Simon Huck. She mentions that she received a phone call from her publicist, asking her to comment on previous speculation that Kardashian and the Blink-182 drummer were living separately and planning to split.

Kardashian called the claims "speculated rumors."

"I go, 'Tell them to print it. See what happens,'" she recalled.

"I was just like, 'They know it's not true. They know they saw a dumb TikTok of someone who makes up fabricated stories,'" Kardashian continued.

Huck agreed, noting he often sees "crazy, weird conspiracy theories" about Kardashian and her famous family.

"People believe it," Kardashian said of the gossip, which is sometimes fueled by AI-generated clips. It is "so bizarre."

Moments later, Kardashian, Huck, and her stepson, Landon Barker, pulled up to her longtime Calabasas home, which is undergoing a major renovation.

In the scene, Kardashian said she expected they were about six months away from being able to move back in. But she was beginning to second-guess that timeline after seeing how few changes had been made since her last visit.

"It's a really vulnerable feeling to have all of the walls of your home ripped apart. There's no electrical. There's nothing," she said in a confessional interview during the episode. "It's like a very vulnerable feeling."

While the renovation was in too early a stage to gather much about Kardashian's design plans, she did bring the cameras through a guest room that she said was going to be for Landon, before he moved into a place of his own.

The 23-year-old rapper was quick to pipe up and claim the space, however, saying that he'd love to have his own space because his current residence is a rental.

Barker and Kardashian have a large blended family of seven children. In November 2023, they welcomed a son, Rocky Thirteen Barker. Before their marriage in 2022, Kardashian had three children with her ex Scott Disick: Mason Disick, 16, Penelope Disick, 14, and Reign Disick, 11.

In addition to Landon, Barker and his ex Shanna Moakler are parents to a 20-year-old daughter, Alabama Barker. The musician also has a stepdaughter—Atiana De La Hoya, 27, whom Moakler had with boxer Oscar De La Hoya.

When asked if she was planning to house the couple's entire family under one roof, Kardashian appeared to have mixed feelings.

"I love it in theory, but I think it's really hard with everybody of all different ages," she said. "It's a much different balance."

Although all of the children may not end up living in the home full time, Kardashian confirmed there will be plenty of space for everyone to make memories in one way or another.

"We're working toward something amazing," she said. "I can't wait to cook and have movie nights, barbecues. I want to make it feel magical for everybody. It's so fun."

Kardashian and Barker have previously opened up about the arrangements they've made to suit their large family. In a 2024 episode of "The Kardashians," which was filmed when she was pregnant with Rocky in 2023, she discussed their plans to move into Barker's nearby Calabasas estate.

"We're going to move into his house, which is a block away, and then redo my house at the same time so that we can all be together, living under one roof with the baby," she said.

Barker opened the doors of that very house to Architectural Digest in May 2022, revealing a surprisingly laid-back aesthetic for a rocker whose vibe typically leans much edgier.

"I've had homes with lots of flashy cars, murals, and bikes hanging from the ceiling. But with three children of my own, plus Kourtney's kids, this place felt right for this moment in my life," he said. "I wanted a house where I can rest and enjoy my family, a place where we can create memories."

#5616. French blood banks hacked amid ‘deeply concerning’ wave of fridge and freezer cyberattacks in Europe

In a recent spate of cyberattacks in Europe against fridges and freezers, the latest assault hit France’s national blood service, where hackers gained control of cold storage systems at medical facilities and turned up the temperature.

The French Blood Establishment, EFS, told media that the facilities managed to save the blood supplies and there has been “no loss of blood products.” But the attacks come after supermarkets in several European countries experienced hacks of their fridges and freezers leading to the loss of millions of Euros in products.

Last month, hackers hit hundreds of supermarkets across France where temperatures were forced up to 50 degrees C overnight in what officials called an “unprecedented” attack. Food losses and fires were reported after “connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France.” What followed was a wave of similar attacks across the continent where fridges and freezers at stores in the U.K., Italy and Germany were recently hacked, following attacks in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine ​consumers’ confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously,” said EU Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.”

Connected fridges can now be controlled and monitored remotely through internet-connected software but with this comes vulnerabilities. Hackers can exploit publicly reachable, legacy or unpatched remote refrigeration management controllers that may use default passwords or weak date-based administrative bypasses.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, told Reuters.

Cybersecurity experts so far have not figured out who’s behind the attacks. Russian hacking groups are a possibility as well as Iranian hacktivists or nation-state hackers. It might also be kids pulling off what have so far been very expensive pranks. Cybersecurity researchers at some firms have installed fake software as honeypots in an attempt to gather information about the hackers.

#5615. How Traton Homes Is Designing for Multigenerational Living

The Presley model's guest suite at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

Today’s buyers are asking their homes to work harder over time. At Traton Homes, main-level guest suites have become an important part of that flexibility, providing space for overnight visitors today and potentially aging parents, caregivers, or other family members in the future.

Director of design Angi Sago explains how evolving household needs are influencing the builder’s approach to floor plans, entertaining spaces, and long-term livability.

Traton offers a variety of floor plans featuring a guest suite on the main. What does that tell you about how buyer priorities are changing?

Buyers are increasingly looking for homes that offer flexibility to accommodate their families’ changing needs. A private guest suite on the main level provides a comfortable space for visiting family and friends, but it also offers the opportunity to accommodate aging parents, whether for extended visits or as a more permanent living arrangement in the future. It’s a feature that adds both immediate convenience and long-term value.

Who are these suites designed for; aging parents, adult children, long-term guests, or a combination?

The Presley model home at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

While these suites certainly provide a wonderful space for overnight guests, we find that many buyers are thinking about aging parents and the possibility of multigenerational living. Having a private guest bedroom with en-suite bath on the main level gives homeowners peace of mind knowing they have a comfortable and accessible space for loved ones, whether they are visiting or eventually become part of the household.

How has demand for multigenerational or guest-friendly living influenced Traton’s floor plans over the past few years?

Traton has recognized the appeal of main-level guest suites for many years, and we’ve incorporated them into our home designs for quite some time. These floor plans have consistently been popular because they offer homeowners flexibility in how they use their space. As families’ needs continue to evolve, we believe this versatility is becoming even more valuable to today’s buyers.

What separates a well-designed guest suite from simply putting an extra bedroom and bathroom on the first floor?

Are buyers looking for spaces that can change purpose over time, such as moving from a guest suite to an aging-in-place bedroom or caregiver space?

Absolutely. Flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a main-level guest suite. A space that initially serves as a bedroom for visiting friends and family can eventually accommodate an aging parent or caregiver. Buyers appreciate knowing their home can adapt to different stages of life without requiring significant changes to the floor plan.

Beyond the guest suite, what design features are becoming more important for homeowners who regularly entertain or host overnight visitors?

Spaces that make entertaining easier and more enjoyable continue to be popular. Butler’s pantries are especially appealing because they can double as a beverage or bar area while providing additional storage and serving space. Keeping rooms are another desirable feature, offering a comfortable, informal gathering area where family and friends can relax and spend time together. Buyers appreciate having spaces that encourage connection while allowing for different types of entertaining.

The Abney model at Linden Grove in Powder Springs, Georgia.

Traton’s floor plans with owner’s suites are offered at various price points. How do expectations for hosting and flexible living differ between by price point, if at all?

Interestingly, we see many of the same priorities across price points. Regardless of price point, homeowners want comfortable, functional spaces where they can welcome family and friends. The primary difference is often the amount of space available for entertaining and the additional features a larger home can accommodate. While buyers of our more expansive homes may have more gathering areas, the desire for a private guest suite and flexible living spaces is equally important to buyers of our more moderately sized plans.

Are buyers willing to give up square footage elsewhere in the home to get a main-level guest suite, larger pantry, loft, or other flexible space?

We find that a main-level guest suite is typically a feature buyers either prioritize from the beginning or don’t necessarily need. Rather than sacrificing square footage elsewhere, buyers tend to gravitate toward floor plans that already incorporate the spaces that matter most to their lifestyle. That’s why offering a variety of thoughtfully designed floor plans is so important. It allows buyers to select a home that best fits their individual needs and preferences.

Looking ahead, how do you expect changing family structures and the way people live together to influence Traton’s next generation of floor plans?

As housing costs continue to put pressure on household budgets, we anticipate that multigenerational living will become an important consideration for home buyers. Sharing a home can offer financial advantages while allowing families to stay connected and support one another. We believe buyers will continue to place a premium on flexible floor plans that provide both shared gathering spaces and private retreats, allowing multiple generations to live comfortably under one roof. At Traton, our goal is to continue designing homes that reflect how families live today while anticipating how their needs may change in the years ahead.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.
